name: कर्मयोग
teaching: Renouncing the world is not the same as renouncing the ego, and stillness of the body is not stillness of the mind. Krishna closes the escape route: no one stays actionless for even a moment, so act — fully, skillfully, as offering — and let the action itself become the discipline. Action is rescued from suspicion: the world itself runs on offered work, and the same deed that binds the grasping hand frees the open one. The chapter ends by naming the real enemy — desire — and the high ground from which it falls.
questions: Where are you performing inaction — appearing detached while the mind churns?
Whose example are you, whether you intend it or not?
Krishna names desire as the enemy 'seated in the senses, mind and intellect.' Where is it seated most firmly in you?

verses.speaker: अर्जुन उवाच
verses.devanagari:
ज्यायसी चेत्कर्मणस्ते मता बुद्धिर्जनार्दन ।
तत्किं कर्मणि घोरे मां नियोजयसि केशव॥
verses.transliteration:
jyāyasī cetkarmaṇaste matā buddhirjanārdana
tatkiṃ karmaṇi ghore māṃ niyojayasi keśava
verses.essence: Arjuna asks: if you hold understanding higher than action, Krishna, why push me into this terrible deed?
verses.translation: If Thou thinkest that knowledge is superior to action, O Krishna, why then, O Kesava, dost Thou ask me to engage in this terrible action?

anvaya.form: adjective, comparative, feminine, nominative singular (agrees with बुद्धिः)
pronoun, 2nd person, genitive singular (of you; 'by you' with a participle)
past passive participle, feminine, nominative singular (is thought)

anvaya.base: जनार्दन · stirrer of people, a name of Krishna
तद् · that; here 'then, in that case'

anvaya.form: adjective, neuter, locative singular (agrees with कर्मणि)

anvaya.base: नि + √युज् · to yoke, to set to (causative)
केशव · fine-haired one, slayer of Keśin, a name of Krishna

verses.explanation: A fair catch. Chapter 2 praised the steady buddhi above all and ended in the still ocean of the sage — and also said 'therefore fight.' Arjuna hears a contradiction and, like every good student, names it. The whole of chapter 3 exists because he refused to nod along.
verses.connection: Answers nothing yet — it questions the join between 2.49 ('action is far inferior') and 2.18/2.37 ('therefore fight').
verses.reflection: When you ask for clarity, check first whether you are seeking light or seeking exit.
verses.background: The second chapter has just ended with high praise of understanding and of the steady sage, after earlier urging Arjuna to fight. Arjuna, standing between the armies at Kurukṣetra, now speaks for the first time since 2.54, and he names the tension he hears in Krishna's teaching.
verses.hook: If knowledge is higher than action, why must Arjuna fight?

views.text: Takes buddhi as knowledge set apart from action, and argues the question only makes sense if knowledge and action were never meant to be combined in one person.
Reads the doubt as: if knowledge, reached by stilling all the senses, alone brings vision of the self, why urge a deed that sets every sense to work and so blocks that vision?

Arjuna infers that knowledge ranks higher from chapter 2's praise of the steady sage and its close 'this is the brahmic state', yet hears 'fight' again and again; hence the question about a violent deed.

Krishna never asked for actions to be given up, only attachment to their fruits. Arjun misread the praise of the intellect as a reason to avoid the grim duty of war, and asks for his doubt to be cleared.

verses.devanagari:
व्यामिश्रेणेव वाक्येन बुद्धिं मोहयसीव मे ।
तदेकं वद निश्चित्य येन श्रेयोऽहमाप्नुयाम्॥
verses.transliteration:
vyāmiśreṇeva vākyena buddhiṃ mohayasīva me
tadekaṃ vada niścitya yena śreyo'hamāpnuyām
verses.essence: With seemingly mixed words you confuse my understanding. Tell me the one thing by which I may reach the highest good.
verses.translation: With this apparently perplexing speech, Thou confusest, as it were, my understanding; therefore tell me that one way for certain by which I may attain bliss.

anvaya.form: relative pronoun, neuter, instrumental singular (by which)

verses.explanation: Twice he says iva — 'as if', 'seemingly' — a student's courtesy: the confusion may be mine, not yours. But his demand is the same as in 2.7: ekam, one thing, decided. The mind in crisis wants a single rope, not a braid of paths.
verses.connection: Restates 2.7's plea for the decisive śreyas, now sharpened by an apparent contradiction in the answer received.
verses.reflection: Bring your real confusion to one trusted person today, phrased as plainly as Arjuna's.
verses.background: Arjuna continues his question. Śrīdhara explains the trouble: Krishna has praised action in one place, such as saying nothing is better for a warrior than a righteous war, and knowledge in another, so Arjuna's mind swings between the two. He now asks for a single answer.
verses.hook: What does Arjuna ask Krishna to do about his confusion?

views.text: Hears Arjuna politely blaming his own dull understanding; if one person cannot follow both, he asks for whichever of knowledge or action suits his capacity and situation.
The question behind both verses: if knowledge is to uproot action entirely, as the wise man casts off good and bad deeds, what use is action at all?
The 'as it were' matters: the supremely compassionate Lord cannot truly bewilder anyone; praise given now to action, now to knowledge only seems confusing through Arjuna's own error.
Arjun feels the teaching on knowledge and on action seems contradictory. Trusting that Krishna is merciful and does not mean to confuse him, he asks for one clear path.

verses.speaker: श्रीभगवानुवाच
verses.devanagari:
लोकेऽस्मिन् द्विविधा निष्ठा पुरा प्रोक्ता मयानघ ।
ज्ञानयोगेन साङ्ख्यानां कर्मयोगेन योगिनाम्॥
verses.transliteration:
loke'smin dvividhā niṣṭhā purā proktā mayānagha
jñānayogena sāṅkhyānāṃ karmayogena yoginām
verses.essence: In this world a twofold path was taught by me of old: the yoga of knowledge for the contemplative, the yoga of action for the active.
verses.translation: In this world there is a twofold path, as I said before, O sinless one; the path of knowledge of the Sankhyas and the path of action of the Yogins.

anvaya.form: pronoun, masculine, locative singular (agrees with लोके)
past passive participle, feminine, nominative singular (was said)
noun, masculine, instrumental singular (by means of)
anvaya.parts: ज्ञान (knowledge) + योग (discipline): 'the discipline that is knowledge'

anvaya.form: noun, masculine, instrumental singular (by means of)
anvaya.parts: कर्म (action) + योग (discipline): 'the discipline that is action'

anvaya.meaning: for the yogis, the men of action

verses.explanation: Krishna's first move is to deny the contradiction: there were never two rival doctrines, only two entrances suited to two temperaments — the reflective and the active. Neither is ranked here; what is ranked is honesty about which kind of person one actually is. Arjuna, archer to the bone, is being quietly told which door is his.
verses.connection: Resolves 3.1–2: the 'mixed words' were two paths for two natures, not one teaching at war with itself.
verses.reflection: Stop comparing your path with another's for one day; both were given by the same teacher.
verses.background: Krishna now replies to Arjuna's complaint about mixed words. Śrīdhara gives the point of the reply: Krishna never taught two separate, rival ways to freedom from which Arjuna must choose one; both lead to the one goal.
verses.hook: What are the two paths Krishna has taught for different kinds of seekers?

views.text: The two steadfastnesses belong to different persons: knowledge for renunciates established in Brahman, action for those engaged in rites. They are not to be combined by one person.
Not everyone seeking release can take up the path of knowledge at once; work done as worship, without desire for fruit, purifies the mind and makes one fit for it.
Takes the line as saying the twofold path was declared to be one, since consciousness itself is made of knowing and acting.
One single commitment to Brahman is taught in two modes by fitness: knowledge for the pure-minded, action for those still purifying. Neither stands on its own.

There are two paths: analytical knowledge of the self for the contemplative, and work done in devotion to God for the active. Work purifies the mind, and knowledge then awakens in it; Krishna addresses both temperaments.

verses.devanagari:
न कर्मणामनारम्भान्नैष्कर्म्यं पुरुषोऽश्नुते ।
न च संन्यसनादेव सिद्धिं समधिगच्छति॥
verses.transliteration:
na karmaṇāmanārambhānnaiṣkarmyaṃ puruṣo'śnute
na ca saṃnyasanādeva siddhiṃ samadhigacchati
verses.essence: Not by abstaining from actions does one attain actionlessness, nor by renunciation alone does one reach perfection.
verses.translation: Not by non-performance of actions does man reach actionlessness; nor by mere renunciation does he attain to perfection.

anvaya.form: noun, masculine, ablative singular (by reason of)
noun, neuter, ablative singular (by means of)

verses.explanation: The first demolition: naiṣkarmya, the state beyond action, is not produced by stopping. An idle body can house a frantic mind; quitting the field is not the same as quitting the fever. The goal is real — but its road runs through action, not around it.
verses.connection: Blocks the exit Arjuna has been eyeing since 1.46: simply not-acting achieves nothing.
verses.reflection: Notice that resigning from action did not resign you from restlessness — the work was never the problem.
verses.background: Having said there are two paths, Krishna turns to the idea that one can simply stop acting. Śrīdhara explains why he does so: the duties of one's station must be done to purify the mind until knowledge dawns, since without that purity knowledge never arises.
verses.hook: Can you become free just by not acting or by renouncing the world?

views.text: Freedom from action means abiding in the actionless Self. Actions purify the mind and so are the means to it; abstaining from them forfeits the means.
Unless one has first worshipped the Lord through unattached work, old sin is not annulled and steady contemplation of the self is not possible.
Sitting idle is not actionlessness: the mind keeps planning and scheming, and thought is real action. Only knowledge of the Self brings that state.

Mere inaction does not free one from karma, since the mind keeps acting; mere renunciation does not bring knowledge to an impure mind. Both paths need knowledge and purifying action, only in different proportions.

verses.devanagari:
न हि कश्चित्क्षणमपि जातु तिष्ठत्यकर्मकृत् ।
कार्यते ह्यवशः कर्म सर्वः प्रकृतिजैर्गुणैः॥
verses.transliteration:
na hi kaścitkṣaṇamapi jātu tiṣṭhatyakarmakṛt
kāryate hyavaśaḥ karma sarvaḥ prakṛtijairguṇaiḥ
verses.essence: No one ever rests even a moment without acting; all are driven helplessly to act by the gunas born of nature.
verses.translation: Verily none can ever remain for even a moment without performing action; for everyone is made to act helplessly indeed by the qualities born of Nature.

anvaya.form: noun, masculine, accusative singular (for a span of time)

anvaya.base: अकर्मकृत् · one who does no action
anvaya.parts: अ (not) + कर्म (action) + कृत् (doer): 'not a doer of action'

anvaya.form: verb, present, causative passive, 3rd person singular (is made to do)
adjective, masculine, instrumental plural (agrees with गुणैः)

verses.explanation: Deeper still: total inaction is not merely useless — it is impossible. Na hi kaścit kṣaṇam api — not even for a moment does anyone remain without acting. Breath, thought, digestion, the flicker of attention: the guṇas born of prakṛti keep every embodied being in motion, avaśaḥ, without asking leave. The choice was never action versus rest; it is only conscious action versus driven action — whether the motion is owned and aimed. The verse is the Gita's refusal of the fantasy of neutrality.
verses.connection: Grounds 3.4 in physiology and physics: the renunciate's stillness is an optical illusion.
verses.reflection: Watch yourself for five minutes: breath, blinking, thought — action never paused. Make peace with the engine.
verses.background: Krishna has said that abstaining from action does not bring freedom from action. Śrīdhara says this verse shows why: renouncing action can only mean giving up attachment, since giving up action itself is impossible.
verses.hook: Is it actually possible to stop acting altogether?

refs.note: No one can stay inactive even for a moment; everyone is driven to act by their own natural qualities.

views.text: Supplies 'the unenlightened' after 'everyone': the knower, who never moves from the Self, is not shaken by the guṇas, so karma-yoga is meant only for those without knowledge.
Body, speech and mind are by nature a constant throbbing; so the action contained within knowledge cannot be avoided, and knowledge and action form one thing.
No one, knower or ignorant, can stay without action even a moment; so renouncing actions can only mean not clinging to them, not giving them up in form.

All activity of body, mind, and speech counts as action. Even in sleep the mind dreams and the organs work, so complete inactivity is impossible; the three qualities of nature compel every being to act.

verses.devanagari:
कर्मेन्द्रियाणि संयम्य य आस्ते मनसा स्मरन् ।
इन्द्रियार्थान्विमूढात्मा मिथ्याचारः स उच्यते॥
verses.transliteration:
karmendriyāṇi saṃyamya ya āste manasā smaran
indriyārthānvimūḍhātmā mithyācāraḥ sa ucyate
verses.essence: One who restrains the organs of action but sits remembering sense-objects in the mind — that deluded one is called a hypocrite.
verses.translation: He who, restraining the organs of action, sits thinking of the sense-objects in mind, he of deluded understanding is called a hypocrite.

anvaya.base: कर्मेन्द्रिय · organ of action (hands, feet, speech…)

anvaya.form: present participle, masculine, nominative singular (while remembering)

anvaya.parts: विमूढ (deluded) + आत्मन् (self, mind): 'one whose mind is deluded'
मिथ्या (false) + आचार (conduct): 'one whose conduct is false'

anvaya.form: verb, present passive, 3rd person singular (is called)

verses.explanation: The portrait everyone recognizes: the body in the posture of a saint, the mind running a cinema of everything renounced. The Gita's word is harsh — mithyācāra, false conduct — because the show deceives its own performer first. Repression is not renunciation; it is desire gone underground.
verses.connection: The dark example proving 3.4–5: outer stopping with inner churning is the worst of both paths.
verses.reflection: Find one renunciation in your life that is really suppression — outward stillness, inward replay.
verses.background: Krishna has just said no one can stop acting even for a moment. Śrīdhara notes that he now censures the ignorant person who gives up action anyway, describing what such outward renunciation turns into.
verses.hook: What do you call someone who renounces outwardly but dwells on pleasures inwardly?

views.text: One who restrains the hands and other organs of action yet keeps recalling sense objects in his mind is of deluded mind, called a hypocrite and a sinful person.
Pictures someone attempting the path of knowledge before his sins are annulled: senses unconquered, mind dragged toward objects, so his practice contradicts his profession and he is lost.
If he does not act with the organs of action he necessarily acts with the mind, because mental action can never be stopped completely.
The hypocrite sits under the pretext of meditating on the Lord while actually recalling sense objects; an impure mind cannot settle on the Self.
Outward renunciation without inner withdrawal is hypocrisy, so honest work in the world is better than false asceticism. The story of two brothers shows that what counts is where the mind dwells.

verses.devanagari:
यस्त्विन्द्रियाणि मनसा नियम्यारभतेऽर्जुन ।
कर्मेन्द्रियैः कर्मयोगमसक्तः स विशिष्यते॥
verses.transliteration:
yastvindriyāṇi manasā niyamyārabhate'rjuna
karmendriyaiḥ karmayogamasaktaḥ sa viśiṣyate
verses.essence: But one who governs the senses by the mind and engages the organs of action in karma-yoga, unattached — that one excels.
verses.translation: But whosoever, controlling the senses by the mind, O Arjuna, engages himself in Karma Yoga with the organs of action, without attachment, he excels.

anvaya.form: verb, present passive, 3rd person singular (is distinguished, excels)

verses.explanation: The mirror image: control on the inside, engagement on the outside — exactly inverted from 3.6. Mastery is proven in motion, not in posture. The unattached doer outranks the attached abstainer.
verses.connection: Answers 3.6 point for point and crowns the working person over the false renunciate.
verses.reflection: Engage one task today with governed senses and an open hand, and feel the difference from grim duty.
verses.background: After censuring the person who stops the body but not the mind, Krishna describes the opposite kind of person. Śrīdhara introduces this verse simply as that contrast: the one who acts is the better.
verses.hook: Who does better than the one who merely sits still?

views.text: The one praised is the unenlightened person eligible for action; he excels the hypocrite of the previous verse.
The karma-yogi excels even one following the path of knowledge: his path suits senses already inclined to act, and he runs no risk of a fall.
While he works, his knowledge is not lost; with the mind not engaged, he acts like a machine-man.
A karma yogi does worldly duties with the body while keeping the mind attached to God. Since attachment to fruits, not action, binds, such a householder surpasses the false renunciant.

verses.devanagari:
नियतं कुरु कर्म त्वं कर्म ज्यायो ह्यकर्मणः ।
शरीरयात्रापि च ते न प्रसिद्ध्येदकर्मणः॥
verses.transliteration:
niyataṃ kuru karma tvaṃ karma jyāyo hyakarmaṇaḥ
śarīrayātrāpi ca te na prasiddhyedakarmaṇaḥ
verses.essence: Perform your allotted action, for action is better than inaction; even the body's journey cannot be sustained without action.
verses.translation: Do thou perform (thy) bounden duty, for action is superior to inaction and even the maintenance of the body would not be possible for thee by inaction.

anvaya.form: past passive participle used as adjective, neuter, accusative singular

verses.explanation: From argument to instruction: niyataṁ kuru karma — do what is yours to do. The clinching point is humble and unanswerable: even the renunciate must eat, and eating is action. Since acting is mandatory, the only open question is its quality.
verses.connection: Converts 3.4–7 into the chapter's first command — and quietly answers 3.1: this is the 'one thing'.
verses.reflection: Do the next required thing without the meeting about whether to do it.
verses.background: Krishna has set the unattached worker above the false renouncer. Drawing the conclusion, he now turns to Arjuna directly with a command, giving his reasons in the same breath.
verses.hook: Why is doing your duty better than doing nothing?

views.text: Niyatam karma means the obligatory daily duties, which scripture does not tie to any particular reward.
'Inaction' here means the path of knowledge itself; even someone fit for it does better with karma-yoga, which is easier, comes naturally and already includes knowledge of the self.
Until the mind is absorbed in God, dutiful work purifies it. Laziness is a great enemy; even caring for the body requires work, and a healthy body helps spiritual life.

verses.devanagari:
यज्ञार्थात्कर्मणोऽन्यत्र लोकोऽयं कर्मबन्धनः ।
तदर्थं कर्म कौन्तेय मुक्तसङ्गः समाचर॥
verses.transliteration:
yajñārthātkarmaṇo'nyatra loko'yaṃ karmabandhanaḥ
tadarthaṃ karma kaunteya muktasaṅgaḥ samācara
verses.essence: Except action done as sacrifice, this world is bound by action. For that purpose, Kaunteya, act free of attachment.
verses.translation: The world is bound by actions other than those performed for the sake of sacrifice; do thou, therefore, O son of Kunti (Arjuna), perform action for that sake (for sacrifice alone), free from attachment.

anvaya.meaning: done for the sake of sacrifice
anvaya.base: यज्ञार्थ · having sacrifice as its purpose
anvaya.form: adjective, neuter, ablative singular (with अन्यत्र: other than)
noun, neuter, ablative singular (with अन्यत्र: other than)

anvaya.base: कर्मबन्धन · having action as its bond
anvaya.parts: कर्म (action) + बन्धन (bond): 'one whose bond is action'

anvaya.base: तदर्थ · for the sake of that
मुक्तसङ्ग · one whose attachment is released
सम् + आ + √चर् · to carry out, conduct

verses.explanation: Here is the chapter's master-key: yajña. Action binds — except action done yajñārtham, for the sake of sacrifice. The same deed, pointed at oneself, forges a chain; pointed beyond oneself, it forges nothing. The old ritual word is being widened: any act done as offering escapes the binding law, and across the next verses the word grows from the fire altar into a whole cosmology of exchange. The instruction itself is plain: mukta-saṅgaḥ samācara — act fully, with the grip released.
verses.connection: Qualifies 3.8: act, yes — but the only unbinding mode of action is the sacrificial one.
verses.reflection: Convert one chore today into yajna: same motions, offered, and watch the binding loosen.
verses.background: Krishna has just told Arjuna to act. Śrīdhara points to the objection in view: some teachers say every action binds and so none should be done. Krishna answers by naming the one kind of action that does not bind.
verses.hook: How can you work without your work binding you?

refs.note: Householders who perform all work as an offering to Viṣṇu and spend spare time on his glories are not bound by their homes or actions.

views.text: Yajña here means God, on the Vedic text 'sacrifice is verily Viṣṇu'; whatever is done for Him does not bind.
Work binds only when done for personal ends; even earning money, if done for scriptural sacrifices without attachment, leads the Lord to grant the vision of the self.
Yajñārtha means action that must necessarily be done; such action, performed without attachment to fruit, yields no binding result.
Work is neither good nor bad in itself; motive decides. Work for one's own senses binds, while work offered as sacrifice to God frees, seeing everything as his, as King Raghu did in giving all away.

verses.devanagari:
सहयज्ञाः प्रजाः सृष्ट्वा पुरोवाच प्रजापतिः ।
अनेन प्रसविष्यध्वमेष वोऽस्त्विष्टकामधुक्॥
verses.transliteration:
sahayajñāḥ prajāḥ sṛṣṭvā purovāca prajāpatiḥ
anena prasaviṣyadhvameṣa vo'stviṣṭakāmadhuk
verses.essence: Having created beings together with sacrifice, Prajapati said of old: by this shall you multiply; let this be your wish-fulfilling cow.
verses.translation: The Creator, having in the beginning (of creation) created mankind together with sacrifice, said, "By this shall ye propagate; let this be the milch cow of your desires (the cow which yields all the desired objects)."

anvaya.form: adjective, feminine, accusative plural (agrees with प्रजाः)
anvaya.parts: सह (with) + यज्ञ (sacrifice): 'having sacrifice along with them'
इष्ट (desired) + काम (object of desire) + धुक् (milker, √दुह्): 'that which milks out what is wished for'

verses.explanation: A creation story with a design principle: sacrifice was not added to the world, it was shipped with it — saha-yajñāḥ, beings born bundled with the mechanism of mutual offering. The cosmos is a gift economy by manufacture. Kāmadhuk, the cow of plenty, milks only for those who feed her.
verses.connection: Begins the cosmological backing (3.10–16) for the yajna-rule of 3.9.
verses.reflection: Treat your work as participation in an old exchange — you were issued breath; issue something back.
verses.background: Krishna has said only action done as sacrifice frees. Now, Śrīdhara says, he shows from the Creator's own words that the one who acts is best, over four verses. This first verse recalls the beginning of creation, when beings were made together with sacrifice.
verses.hook: What did the Creator give beings at the beginning, along with sacrifice?

views.text: At creation Prajāpati made the people of the three castes together with sacrifices and told them to grow by sacrifice; 'milch cow of desires' means that which yields coveted objects, particular results.
Prajāpati is Nārāyaṇa, who out of compassion for beings sunk in matter created them with sacrifice as His worship, so it could yield release and the aims in keeping with it.
Creatures were made together with action; action yields either rebirth or emancipation, rebirth through attachment and emancipation through freedom from it.
Sacrifice here stands for all obligatory works; praising rites done for desired results still serves the point that action is better than inaction.
Every part of creation draws from the whole and gives back to it. Like a hand serving the body, humans fulfil their own good by doing their duties as an offering to God.

verses.devanagari:
देवान्भावयतानेन ते देवा भावयन्तु वः ।
परस्परं भावयन्तः श्रेयः परमवाप्स्यथ॥
verses.transliteration:
devānbhāvayatānena te devā bhāvayantu vaḥ
parasparaṃ bhāvayantaḥ śreyaḥ paramavāpsyatha
verses.essence: Nourish the gods with this, and may the gods nourish you; nourishing one another, you shall attain the highest good.
verses.translation: With this do ye nourish the gods and may those gods nourish you; thus nourishing one another, ye shall attain to the highest good.

anvaya.base: √भू · to be (causative: to cause to thrive, nourish)

anvaya.form: present participle, causative, masculine, nominative plural (while nourishing)
adjective, neuter, accusative singular (agrees with श्रेयः)

verses.explanation: The verb bhāvayata — cause to be, sustain, cherish — runs both directions: humans sustain the powers (rain, sun, soil, the unseen agencies of the world), and the powers sustain humans. Reality is a circulation, and parasparam — 'one another' — is its law. Śreyas, Arjuna's sought-for good, turns out to live inside the loop, not outside it.
verses.connection: Unpacks Prajapati's promise of 3.10 as reciprocity — the world as a two-way feeding.
verses.reflection: Nourish one system that nourishes you — a person, a place, a practice — before withdrawing from it again.
verses.background: Krishna is still reporting what the Creator said to the first beings. Śrīdhara frames this verse as the answer to a question left by the last: how is sacrifice to give people what they wish for?
verses.hook: How do humans and the gods support one another?

refs.note: Worshipping Viṣṇu automatically worships all the gods, since they draw their power from him.

views.text: The gods are Indra and the rest, who repay with rain; the supreme good is liberation through knowledge, or heaven, depending on what the aspirant seeks.
The gods form the Lord's body and have Him as their Self, so sacrifice offered to them is worship of Him.
Reads the devas as the deities of the senses: feed them their objects, and they in turn let you rest in the Self, through alternating outward activity and meditation.

The celestial gods are souls holding offices in running the universe, not God himself. Sacrifice offered to the Supreme pleases them all, as watering a tree's root nourishes every branch, and they in turn bring prosperity.

verses.devanagari:
इष्टान्भोगान्हि वो देवा दास्यन्ते यज्ञभाविताः ।
तैर्दत्तानप्रदायैभ्यो यो भुङ्क्ते स्तेन एव सः॥
verses.transliteration:
iṣṭānbhogānhi vo devā dāsyante yajñabhāvitāḥ
tairdattānapradāyaibhyo yo bhuṅkte stena eva saḥ
verses.essence: Nourished by sacrifice, the gods will give you the enjoyments you desire. One who enjoys their gifts without offering back is simply a thief.
verses.translation: The gods, nourished by the sacrifice, will give you the desired objects. So, he who enjoys the objects given by the gods without offering (in return) to them, is verily a thief.

anvaya.form: past participle used as adjective, masculine, accusative plural (agrees with भोगान्)
adjective, masculine, nominative plural (agrees with देवाः)
past passive participle, masculine, accusative plural (things given)

verses.explanation: The strongest word yet: stena, thief. Everything consumed — air, grain, language, safety — arrived through the labor of forces and beings one did not create. To take from the circulation without returning to it is not neutrality; it is theft with extra steps. The verse turns gratitude from a sentiment into an accounting.
verses.connection: The shadow side of 3.11's loop: opt out of giving while continuing to take, and you have a name.
verses.reflection: Name three things you consumed today and what you returned for them; settle one account.
verses.background: Continuing the Creator's words about sacrifice, Krishna makes the earlier promise explicit. Śrīdhara says that in doing so he states the fault of not acting: what to call the one who takes the gods' gifts and gives nothing back.
verses.hook: Who is called a thief for enjoying nature's gifts?

views.text: The thief is one who gratifies only his own body and senses without repaying his debts to the gods through sacrifice.
Theft is taking as one's own and using for oneself what was given for another's purpose; gifts meant for worship, consumed selfishly, unfit one for release.
The sense-deities bring objects to mind; enjoying them without offering is deceit. Enjoy what comes only to calm the senses' restlessness.
Everything belongs to God. Using his creation for our own pleasure without acknowledging him is theft in his eyes, even for someone who lives decently but ignores him.

verses.devanagari:
यज्ञशिष्टाशिनः सन्तो मुच्यन्ते सर्वकिल्बिषैः ।
भुञ्जते ते त्वघं पापा ये पचन्त्यात्मकारणात्॥
verses.transliteration:
yajñaśiṣṭāśinaḥ santo mucyante sarvakilbiṣaiḥ
bhuñjate te tvaghaṃ pāpā ye pacantyātmakāraṇāt
verses.essence: The good who eat the remnants of sacrifice are freed from all sins; the wicked who cook for themselves alone eat sin.
verses.translation: The righteous who eat the remnants of the sacrifice are freed from all sins; but those sinful ones who cook food (only) for their own sake verily eat sin.

anvaya.meaning: who eat the remnants of sacrifice
anvaya.base: यज्ञशिष्टाशिन् · eater of what remains after sacrifice
anvaya.parts: यज्ञ (sacrifice) + शिष्ट (remainder) + आशिन् (eater): 'eaters of what is left after sacrifice'

anvaya.form: verb, present passive, 3rd person plural (are released)
adjective used as noun, masculine, nominative plural
noun, neuter, ablative singular (for the sake of)

verses.explanation: Two meals, identical on the plate: one is leftover from an offering, eaten last after the world has been fed; the other is cooked ātma-kāraṇāt, for me first. The food is the same — the direction of the life around it differs, and that direction is what is actually swallowed. 'They eat sin' is the Gita's most vivid sentence about consumption.
verses.connection: Brings 3.12's theft down to the dinner table: the daily test of whether one lives inside or outside the loop.
verses.reflection: Before eating today, offer the meal mentally first — then notice the taste of unstolen food.
verses.background: Krishna has just named the person who enjoys without offering a thief. Closing this four-verse account, he draws the contrast at the level of daily food. Śrīdhara relates it to a householder's daily offerings, which cleanse the faults of ordinary household work.
verses.hook: Why does eating food first offered in sacrifice free you from sin?

views.text: The remnants free one from the sins of the household's 'slaughter-places' (oven, water-pot, cutting and grinding tools, broom), which the five daily offerings atone.
Those who acquire and cook food only to worship the Lord dwelling in the gods, and live on what remains, are cleansed of the impurities blocking vision of the self.
Those who enjoy objects only as a means of resting in the Self are freed from both merit and demerit; those who make enjoyment the goal gain 'sin' in the form of good and bad alike.
Food cooked and offered to God first becomes his grace, and eating it frees one from sin; eating only for oneself incurs sin. The commentary also argues for a vegetarian diet.

verses.devanagari:
अन्नाद्भवन्ति भूतानि पर्जन्यादन्नसम्भवः ।
यज्ञाद्भवति पर्जन्यो यज्ञः कर्मसमुद्भवः॥
verses.transliteration:
annādbhavanti bhūtāni parjanyādannasambhavaḥ
yajñādbhavati parjanyo yajñaḥ karmasamudbhavaḥ
verses.essence: From food beings arise; from rain, food; from sacrifice, rain; and sacrifice is born of action.
verses.translation: From food come forth beings; from rain food is produced; from sacrifice arises rain and sacrifice is born of action.

anvaya.base: कर्मसमुद्भव · having action as its source
anvaya.parts: कर्म (action) + समुद्भव (origin): 'that whose origin is action'

verses.explanation: The chain of the world traced backward: creatures ← food ← rain ← sacrifice ← action. Read it as ecology before the word existed: life depends on cycles, cycles depend on inputs, and human action is one of the inputs. The startling link is yajñāt parjanyaḥ — offering sustains the very weather; the moral economy and the natural economy are one system.
verses.connection: Supplies the supply-chain behind 3.11–13: why withholding one's action starves the whole circuit.
verses.reflection: Trace your lunch backward: rain, soil, hands, transport. Eat one bite for everyone in the chain.
verses.background: Krishna gives a further reason to act: action keeps the wheel of the world turning. Śrīdhara notes this is argued over three verses. This first one traces the cycle from food back toward action.
verses.hook: How is sacrifice linked to the food that sustains all life?

views.text: Sacrifice here means its unseen result (apūrva), produced by the priest's and sacrificer's acts; the link to rain follows the smṛti that oblations reach the sun, which gives rain.
Food making beings and rain making food are common experience; that sacrifice brings rain is known from scripture; sacrifice itself springs from the agent's activity.
Reads the chain inwardly: food is the undivided object of enjoyment, the rain-cloud is the Self as enjoyer, and sacrifice is the act of enjoying, rooted in the freedom of action-energy.

verses.devanagari:
कर्म ब्रह्मोद्भवं विद्धि ब्रह्माक्षरसमुद्भवम् ।
तस्मात्सर्वगतं ब्रह्म नित्यं यज्ञे प्रतिष्ठितम्॥
verses.transliteration:
karma brahmodbhavaṃ viddhi brahmākṣarasamudbhavam
tasmātsarvagataṃ brahma nityaṃ yajñe pratiṣṭhitam
verses.essence: Know action to arise from Brahman, and Brahman from the Imperishable; therefore the all-pervading Brahman is ever established in sacrifice.
verses.translation: Know thou that action comes from Brahma and Brahma comes from the Imperishable. Therefore, the all-pervading (Brahma) ever rests in sacrifice.

anvaya.base: ब्रह्मोद्भव · having Brahman as its source
anvaya.parts: ब्रह्म (Brahman, the Veda) + उद्भव (origin): 'that whose source is Brahman'
अक्षर (imperishable) + समुद्भव (origin): 'that whose source is the Imperishable'

anvaya.form: past passive participle, neuter, nominative singular (is established)

verses.explanation: The chain's final links reach the source: right action flows from Brahman — here the Veda, the articulated order — which itself flows from the Akshara, the Imperishable. Sacrifice is therefore not a human invention bolted onto reality; it is the point where the Absolute touches the working world. To act sacrificially is to stand where the current enters.
verses.connection: Completes the regression of 3.14 to its origin, sanctifying the whole cycle.
verses.reflection: Your smallest duty is plugged into the largest circuit; do it once today with that voltage in mind.
verses.background: Krishna continues the cycle traced in the last verse, which ended with sacrifice born of action. This verse follows the chain further back, past action to its source. Śrīdhara reads the first link as the Veda, which comes from the Imperishable.
verses.hook: Where do prescribed duties come from, and where is God present in them?

refs.note: The four Vedas came forth as the breath of the Supreme Being.
The saying that sacrifice is truly Viṣṇu himself identifies the act of offering with God.
Krishna tells Uddhav that he himself is sacrifice.

views.text: Brahma here is the Veda, breathed out by the Imperishable; it is 'all-pervading' because it reveals everything, and rests on sacrifice because sacrificial injunctions dominate it.
Brahma means the body made of prakṛti, and the Imperishable is the individual self dwelling in it; so all bodies, the instruments of action, are rooted in sacrifice.
The all-pervading Imperishable is said to be 'established in sacrifice' because sacrifice is the means by which it is reached.
The Vedas came from God's breath and set out duties that lift people gradually toward goodness. Duties offered to him as sacrifice become godly, because God himself is present in sacrifice.

verses.devanagari:
एवं प्रवर्तितं चक्रं नानुवर्तयतीह यः ।
अघायुरिन्द्रियारामो मोघं पार्थ स जीवति॥
verses.transliteration:
evaṃ pravartitaṃ cakraṃ nānuvartayatīha yaḥ
aghāyurindriyārāmo moghaṃ pārtha sa jīvati
verses.essence: One who does not turn this turning wheel, living in sin, delighting in the senses — that one lives in vain, Partha.
verses.translation: He who does not follow here the wheel thus set revolving, who is of sinful life, rejoicing in the senses, he lives in vain, O Arjuna.

anvaya.base: प्र + √वृत् · to turn (causative: to set turning)
anvaya.form: past passive participle, neuter, accusative singular (agrees with चक्रम्)

anvaya.parts: अघ (sin) + आयुस् (life): 'one whose life is sinful'

anvaya.base: इन्द्रियाराम · whose pleasure-garden is the senses
anvaya.parts: इन्द्रिय (sense) + आराम (delight): 'one who takes pleasure in the senses'

verses.explanation: The cosmology gets its verdict. The wheel — beings, food, rain, offering, action — turns whether one joins it or not; the only choice is to turn with it or to free-ride. Moghaṁ jīvati: such a life is not condemned to torment so much as to pointlessness — a cog that takes the rotation and returns nothing.
verses.connection: Seals the yajna section (3.10–16) with its judgment, before the great exception of the next verse.
verses.reflection: Ask honestly where you are drawing from the common wheel without turning it.
verses.background: Krishna has traced the whole wheel back to its divine source. Since the Lord himself set it turning for the good of beings, Śrīdhara says, this last of the three verses gives the verdict on the one who will not turn it.
verses.hook: What does it mean to live in vain, according to this verse?

views.text: Closes the argument: until fit for knowledge, a qualified but unenlightened person must take up karma-yoga; it then raises who, if anyone, is exempt.
Applies to every practitioner, of action or of knowledge: one who does not live on the remnants of sacrifice lets rajas and tamas grow, and his effort toward the self is fruitless.
The wheel runs from the Lord's word, the Veda, to people's action, then to rain, food and beings, who act again; whoever does not keep it turning lives uselessly.
Humans alone can choose whether to play their part in the cosmic cycle. Societies that honour it flourish; those who refuse their sacrifice become slaves of the senses and waste their lives.

verses.devanagari:
यस्त्वात्मरतिरेव स्यादात्मतृप्तश्च मानवः ।
आत्मन्येव च सन्तुष्टस्तस्य कार्यं न विद्यते॥
verses.transliteration:
yastvātmaratireva syādātmatṛptaśca mānavaḥ
ātmanyeva ca santuṣṭastasya kāryaṃ na vidyate
verses.essence: But the one who delights in the Self alone, satisfied and content in the Self — for that one no duty exists.
verses.translation: But for that man who rejoices only in the Self, who is satisfied with the Self and who is content in the Self alone, verily there is nothing to do.

anvaya.base: आत्मरति · one whose delight is the Self
anvaya.parts: आत्मन् (Self) + रति (delight): 'one who delights in the Self'

anvaya.base: आत्मतृप्त · one satisfied by the Self

anvaya.form: gerundive, neuter, nominative singular (what must be done)
verb, present passive, 3rd person singular (is found)

verses.explanation: Honesty compels the exception: there exists a person beyond the wheel — one whose delight, satisfaction, and contentment have all moved house into the Self. For such a one the machinery of obligation has nothing left to leverage; duty presupposes a lack, and the lack is gone. The bar, note, is total: rati, tṛpti, santoṣa, all three, all inward.
verses.connection: The honest asterisk on 3.16's wheel: it binds everyone except the truly full — described in 2.55.
verses.reflection: Glimpse the person who needs nothing from the day — then return to your day a little lighter.
verses.background: Krishna has taught action as the way for those not yet free, to purify the mind. Śrīdhara says he now turns, over two verses, to the knower, for whom action has no further use. This first verse describes who that knower is.
verses.hook: Is there anyone who no longer has any duty to perform?

views.text: The person meant is the renunciate steadfast in Self-knowledge; delight, satisfaction and contentment all in the Self show he depends on no outer object.
For one whose vision of the self no longer needs any means, with the self alone as his sustenance, nourishment and enjoyment, nothing remains to be done to gain that vision.
Only those free of material desire can be content in the self. Such God-realized souls have reached the goal the Vedic duties serve, like a graduate no longer bound by student rules.

verses.devanagari:
नैव तस्य कृतेनार्थो नाकृतेनेह कश्चन ।
न चास्य सर्वभूतेषु कश्चिदर्थव्यपाश्रयः॥
verses.transliteration:
naiva tasya kṛtenārtho nākṛteneha kaścana
na cāsya sarvabhūteṣu kaścidarthavyapāśrayaḥ
verses.essence: Such a one has no purpose in what is done or left undone here, nor any need to depend on any being for anything.
verses.translation: For him there is no interest whatever in what is done or what is not done; nor does he depend on any being for any object.

anvaya.form: past passive participle as noun, neuter, instrumental singular (by)
past passive participle as noun, neuter, instrumental singular (by)
pronoun, masculine, genitive singular (of/for this one)

anvaya.parts: अर्थ (purpose) + व्यपाश्रय (reliance): 'relying on someone for an end'

verses.explanation: The exception drawn to its logical edge: for the Self-content, both columns of the ledger — done and not-done — read zero, and no being holds anything they need. This is not license but diagnosis: action loses its grip exactly when nothing is wanted from it. Which raises the question the next verse must answer — then why would such a person ever act?
verses.connection: Completes 3.17; the freed one owes the wheel nothing — setting up the deeper reason for action in 3.19–20.
verses.reflection: Imagine acting with nothing to gain and nothing to lose — then borrow that posture for one hour.
verses.background: Krishna has just said the one content in the Self has nothing to do. Śrīdhara introduces this verse as the reason for that statement: what doing and not doing mean, or fail to mean, for such a person.
verses.hook: Does someone at peace in the self gain anything from acting or not?

views.text: No sin comes to him from non-performance, and he depends on no being, from Brahmā down to a plant, for any end that action might secure.
Only the one already established needs no means; for every seeker karma-yoga stays better, being easy, safe from error, and containing contemplation of the self.
Even the gods, who might obstruct liberation, cannot hinder such a knower, since he becomes their very Self; so he needs no rites to placate them.

Self-realized souls are directly engaged in devotion, so dropping worldly duties is no sin for them. Some saints kept their duties as karma yogis, others renounced them; both choices are open to the sage.

verses.devanagari:
तस्मादसक्तः सततं कार्यं कर्म समाचर ।
असक्तो ह्याचरन्कर्म परमाप्नोति पूरुषः॥
verses.transliteration:
tasmādasaktaḥ satataṃ kāryaṃ karma samācara
asakto hyācarankarma paramāpnoti pūruṣaḥ
verses.essence: Therefore, unattached, ever perform the action that must be done; for acting without attachment one attains the Supreme.
verses.translation: Therefore without attachment, do thou always perform action which should be done; for by performing action without attachment man reaches the Supreme.

anvaya.form: gerundive, neuter, accusative singular (to be done)
present participle, masculine, nominative singular (while performing)
adjective used as noun, neuter, accusative singular (object)

verses.explanation: The 'therefore' lands on Arjuna, who is not yet the exception of 3.17–18. For the climber, unattached action is itself the rope: asakto hy ācaran karma param āpnoti — doing without attachment reaches the very Supreme. The path and the summit use the same muscle. Note the pairing in tasmād asaktaḥ satataṃ … samācara: detachment goes with constancy and thoroughness, not with half-heartedness. The released hand grips the tool better than the anxious one.
verses.connection: Returns from the liberated exception (3.17–18) to the seeker's rule: act, but unhooked.
verses.reflection: Therefore, without attachment, do the work in front of you — make this sentence your noon bell.
verses.background: Krishna has described the knower who needs nothing from action. Śaṅkara has him add that Arjuna is not yet established in that fullness, so the exemption does not apply to him, and Krishna draws the conclusion.
verses.hook: What path does Krishna recommend to Arjuna, and why does it lead highest?

views.text: Acting unattached means working as a dedication to God; the Highest is liberation, reached through the purification of the mind.
Work with detachment, regarding yourself as not the doer; the Supreme is reached by karma-yoga itself.
For one who rejoices in the Self, action and non-action do not differ; he acts not for any gain but because the deed deserves doing, and so should one act, unattached.
Although the realized need not do prescribed duties, Krishna advises Arjun to remain a karma yogi rather than renounce action, and gives his reasons in the verses that follow.

verses.devanagari:
कर्मणैव हि संसिद्धिमास्थिता जनकादयः ।
लोकसंग्रहमेवापि सम्पश्यन्कर्तुमर्हसि॥
verses.transliteration:
karmaṇaiva hi saṃsiddhimāsthitā janakādayaḥ
lokasaṃgrahamevāpi sampaśyankartumarhasi
verses.essence: By action alone Janaka and others attained perfection. Even considering the welfare of the world, you should act.
verses.translation: Janaka and others attained perfection verily by action only; even with a view to the protection of the masses thou shouldst perform action.

anvaya.form: noun, neuter, instrumental singular (by means of)
past participle, masculine, nominative plural (having attained)

anvaya.base: जनक + आदि · Janaka and so on
anvaya.parts: जनक (King Janaka) + आदि (beginning): 'those who have Janaka as the first'

anvaya.base: लोकसंग्रह · welfare, holding-together of the world
anvaya.parts: लोक (world, people) + संग्रह (holding together): 'the holding-together of the world'

anvaya.form: present participle, masculine, nominative singular (while considering)

verses.explanation: Precedent and a new word. Janaka — philosopher-king, liberated while ruling — proves the path works at the highest difficulty setting. Then the Gita introduces loka-saṅgraha: the holding-together of the world, the maintenance of the common fabric. A second reason to act enters: not your liberation only, but everyone who is watching how you live.
verses.connection: Backs 3.19 with history and widens its motive from self-perfection to the welfare of all.
verses.reflection: Even the perfected kept working for the world's sake; let loka-sangraha dignify your ordinary Monday.
verses.background: Krishna has told Arjuna to act without attachment. Śrīdhara says he now cites the conduct of the good as proof, naming King Janaka, a famous ruler-sage, and adds a second reason: keeping the world on its course.
verses.hook: Why should even the perfected keep working?

views.text: Offers two readings: if Janaka and others were fully realized, they kept acting from past momentum to keep people from straying; if not, action purified their minds and led them gradually to liberation.
Even those fit for the path of knowledge, like Janaka, foremost of knowers, chose Karma Yoga as the better means to the vision of the self.
Loka-saṅgraha means keeping people in their own dharma: if the knower acts, everyone acts; if he quits, the ignorant would quit too, citing his example.

King Janak reached perfection through his royal duties and kept doing them as an example. When leaders renounce work, unready followers copy them to escape responsibility; when they work, others keep to their duties.

verses.devanagari:
यद्यदाचरति श्रेष्ठस्तत्तदेवेतरो जनः ।
स यत्प्रमाणं कुरुते लोकस्तदनुवर्तते॥
verses.transliteration:
yadyadācarati śreṣṭhastattadevetaro janaḥ
sa yatpramāṇaṃ kurute lokastadanuvartate
verses.essence: Whatever the best person does, others do the same; whatever standard such a one sets, the world follows.
verses.translation: Whatsoever a great man does, that the other men also do; whatever he sets up as the standard, that the world (mankind) follows.

anvaya.form: pronoun, neuter, accusative singular (repetition means 'each and every')
adjective used as noun, masculine, nominative singular (subject)

verses.explanation: The mechanics of loka-saṅgraha in one couplet: people do not follow arguments, they follow examples. The śreṣṭha — whoever stands highest in others' eyes — legislates by behavior whether they intend to or not; whatever such a person takes as the standard, lokas tad anuvartate, the world follows. Arjuna, the most watched warrior alive, cannot resign privately; his exit would be ten thousand exits. Example is the one instruction that reaches everyone, which is why visibility is responsibility.
verses.connection: Explains why 3.20's world-welfare clause binds Arjuna specifically: visibility is responsibility.
verses.reflection: Someone is copying you right now without telling you. Behave accordingly.
verses.background: Krishna has just given the welfare of the world as a reason to act. Śaṅkara has the question asked here: by whom, and how, are people kept from going astray? This verse answers it.
verses.hook: Why do ordinary people copy the actions of great ones?

views.text: Whatever a leader does, his follower does the same, and whatever he upholds as authority, Vedic or secular, the ordinary person accepts as authoritative.

The eminent person is one known for scriptural learning and practice; others copy even the details of his observance, so he must keep his station's duties, or the ruin of those who follow him brings him down too.
Whatever the great person treats as authority, the scripture of action or the scripture of withdrawal, ordinary people take up that same path.
Human beings are imitators: they take their sense of right and wrong from those they regard as morally above them.
People take their standards from the lives of great people, so leaders carry a moral duty to set lofty examples in word, deed, and character; without such leaders society slides into selfishness.

verses.devanagari:
न मे पार्थास्ति कर्तव्यं त्रिषु लोकेषु किञ्चन ।
नानवाप्तमवाप्तव्यं वर्त एव च कर्मणि॥
verses.transliteration:
na me pārthāsti kartavyaṃ triṣu lokeṣu kiñcana
nānavāptamavāptavyaṃ varta eva ca karmaṇi
verses.essence: For me, Partha, there is nothing to be done in the three worlds, nothing unattained to attain — yet I remain in action.
verses.translation: There is nothing in the three worlds, O Arjuna, that should be done by Me, nor is there anything unattained that should be attained; yet I engage Myself in action.

anvaya.form: gerundive, neuter, nominative singular (to be done)
past participle with negative, neuter, nominative singular (not yet gained)
gerundive, neuter, nominative singular (to be gained)

verses.explanation: Krishna offers the ultimate exhibit: himself. Nothing in three worlds is missing from him, no duty can compel him — and he acts anyway, continuously. Action, in its purest case, is not driven by lack at all; it is overflow. The freed do not stop working; they stop needing the work.
verses.connection: Escalates Janaka's example (3.20) to the divine case: even God keeps the wheel turning.
verses.reflection: Do one duty today that you have technically outgrown, simply because others are watching how you live.
verses.background: Krishna has said people follow the example of the great. Śaṅkara has him add: if Arjuna doubts this duty, why not look at Krishna himself? Krishna now offers himself as the example, over three verses beginning here.
verses.hook: Why does Krishna keep acting when he has nothing left to gain?

views.text: Krishna has no duty anywhere in the three worlds, because nothing remains unachieved for him or still to be achieved; even so he continues in action.
The Lord of all, whose desires are fulfilled and whose will is always true, takes forms among gods and men by choice; with nothing to gain by work, he still works for the protection of the world.
Krishna cites himself to show that for one who has gained everything and is fully content, favouring the world is the only remaining reason to act.
We work because we lack bliss, but God is complete in himself and needs nothing. When he acts, it can only be for the welfare of others.

verses.devanagari:
यदि ह्यहं न वर्तेयं जातु कर्मण्यतन्द्रितः ।
मम वर्त्मानुवर्तन्ते मनुष्याः पार्थ सर्वशः॥
verses.transliteration:
yadi hyahaṃ na varteyaṃ jātu karmaṇyatandritaḥ
mama vartmānuvartante manuṣyāḥ pārtha sarvaśaḥ
verses.essence: For if I did not engage tirelessly in action, Partha, people would follow my path in every way.
verses.translation: For, should I not ever engage Myself in action, unwearied, men would in every way follow My path, O Arjuna.

anvaya.form: optative, 1st person singular, middle voice (if I were to)

verses.explanation: Even God is on display. Were Krishna to rest, the resting — not the realization behind it — is what the world would copy. Example transmits the visible, never the invisible; therefore the realized must keep their outsides exemplary for the sake of those who can only see outsides.
verses.connection: Applies 3.21's imitation-law to 3.22's divine actor: his ceaselessness is pedagogy.
verses.reflection: Your slack teaches faster than your speeches; tighten one loose habit the world can see.
verses.background: Krishna has said that though he needs nothing, he keeps acting. Śrīdhara says this verse shows the harm that would follow if he did not: what other people would do in that case.
verses.hook: What would happen if Krishna ever stopped performing his duties?

views.text: If Krishna, being the Highest, ever ceased to act untiringly and vigilantly, people would follow his path in every way.
Born by choice into Vasudeva's virtuous family, Krishna must keep that family's duties; otherwise people would take his idleness as the true way, neglect their duties and fall to ruin.
If the Lord stayed inactive, people would copy him, sink into tamas and pass into inertia.
Playing the role of a royal leader, Krishna knew that if he neglected prescribed duties, lesser people would follow him, and he would be at fault for leading humanity astray.

verses.devanagari:
उत्सीदेयुरिमे लोका न कुर्यां कर्म चेदहम् ।
सङ्करस्य च कर्ता स्यामुपहन्यामिमाः प्रजाः॥
verses.transliteration:
utsīdeyurime lokā na kuryāṃ karma cedaham
saṅkarasya ca kartā syāmupahanyāmimāḥ prajāḥ
verses.essence: These worlds would fall to ruin if I did not perform action; I would be the maker of confusion and destroy these beings.
verses.translation: These worlds would perish if I did not perform action; I should be the author of confusion of castes and destruction of these beings.

anvaya.form: optative, 1st person singular (if I were to do)

verses.explanation: The stakes stated maximally: the divine work-stoppage would unravel worlds. Note the echo — saṅkara, 'confusion', the very word from Arjuna's lament (1.41–42). Arjuna feared that fighting would breed saṅkara; Krishna answers that abandoning one's appointed work is what truly breeds it, at every scale up to the cosmic.
verses.connection: Turns Arjuna's own chapter-one vocabulary against his conclusion: dereliction, not duty, is the destroyer.
verses.reflection: Consider what unravels around you when you stop showing up — then show up.
verses.background: Krishna has said people would follow him if he stopped acting. Śrīdhara frames this verse as the question 'so what?': it ends the three-verse example by spelling out the consequence for the worlds and for the beings in them.
verses.hook: How could the inaction of one great figure throw the world into chaos?

views.text: For God, whose work is helping creatures, to end up destroying them would be unfitting; likewise any knower of the Self has a duty to help others even with no obligation of his own.
Applied to Arjuna: if he, foremost of the virtuous, claimed fitness for the path of knowledge, followers who do not know their own competence would drop Karma Yoga and be lost.
Upahanyām is taken as 'I would defile' these beings: once action lapses, social order mixes, and the one who set the example is its author.

Had Krishna failed in his duties, people imitating him would fall into chaos. Likewise, if the famed Arjun abandoned his duty to protect righteousness, other warriors might follow, harming the innocent.

verses.devanagari:
सक्ताः कर्मण्यविद्वांसो यथा कुर्वन्ति भारत ।
कुर्याद्विद्वांस्तथासक्तश्चिकीर्षुर्लोकसंग्रहम्॥
verses.transliteration:
saktāḥ karmaṇyavidvāṃso yathā kurvanti bhārata
kuryādvidvāṃstathāsaktaścikīrṣurlokasaṃgraham
verses.essence: As the unwise act attached to action, Bharata, so should the wise act unattached, desiring the world's welfare.
verses.translation: As the ignorant men act from attachment to action, O Bharata (Arjuna), so should the wise act without attachment, wishing the welfare of the world.

anvaya.form: adjective used as noun with negative, masculine, nominative plural (subject)
adjective used as noun, masculine, nominative singular (subject)
past participle with negative, masculine, nominative singular (unattached)
desiderative adjective, masculine, nominative singular (wishing to do)

verses.explanation: A precise behavioral prescription: same intensity, different fuel. From the outside, the sage's workday should be indistinguishable from the striver's — equal diligence, equal completeness — with one invisible substitution: loka-saṅgraha where self-interest used to be. Detachment that shows up as sloppiness is not detachment.
verses.connection: Operationalizes 3.20–24: how the knower's action should actually look — exactly like everyone's, minus the hook.
verses.reflection: Match the diligence of the ambitious today, minus the anxiety — same energy, different fuel.
verses.background: Krishna has used his own example to show why the one who needs nothing still acts. Śrīdhara says he now concludes that even the knower of the Self should work out of compassion, for the world's sake, by comparing the knower with the ignorant.
verses.hook: How should the wise act differently from those attached to their work?

refs.note: One should keep performing prescribed duties until one has developed detachment from sense objects and faith in hearing about God.

views.text: The knower acts without the sense of agency and without wanting results; for such a one there is no duty except working so that people do not go astray.
If a learned person dropped action, ordinary people, unable either to give up activity or to enter the stream of wisdom, would lose their footing and grow weak.
The knower keeps acting out of compassion for others (tat-kṛpayā), not from any need of his own.

Ritual-minded people work faithfully for rewards; breaking their faith before they have devotion leaves them nowhere. So the wise should keep working too, without attachment, to set an example and serve society.

verses.devanagari:
न बुद्धिभेदं जनयेदज्ञानां कर्मसङ्गिनाम् ।
जोषयेत्सर्वकर्माणि विद्वान्युक्तः समाचरन्॥
verses.transliteration:
na buddhibhedaṃ janayedajñānāṃ karmasaṅginām
joṣayetsarvakarmāṇi vidvānyuktaḥ samācaran
verses.essence: Let the wise not unsettle the minds of the ignorant attached to action; acting with discipline himself, he should lead them to do all their work gladly.
verses.translation: Let no wise man unsettle the mind of ignorant people who are attached to action; he should engage them in all actions, himself fulfilling them with devotion.

anvaya.base: बुद्धिभेद · split or disturbance of the mind
anvaya.parts: बुद्धि (understanding, conviction) + भेद (breaking): 'a breaking of conviction'

anvaya.base: √जन् · to be born; causative: to produce

anvaya.form: adjective used as noun, masculine, genitive plural (of)
causative optative, 3rd person singular (should cause to)
adjective used as noun, masculine, nominative singular (subject)
past participle, masculine, nominative singular (yoked, steady)
present participle, masculine, nominative singular (while doing)

verses.explanation: A rare ethic of teaching: do not shatter a working person's framework with truths they cannot yet carry. Buddhi-bheda — splitting someone's operating understanding — leaves them with neither their old motivation nor a new one. The wise teach by joṣayet: making good action lovely through visible practice, not by lecturing people out of the only engine they have.
verses.connection: The pedagogical corollary of 3.25: the sage's sameness-in-action protects, rather than disturbs, those still climbing.
verses.reflection: Do not argue someone out of their honest practice today; work beside them instead.
verses.background: Krishna has said the wise should act for the world's sake. Śrīdhara raises an objection: would compassion not rather teach the ignorant the truth directly? This verse is Krishna's answer to that.
verses.hook: Should the wise tell people who work for rewards to stop working?

views.text: The disturbance to avoid is shaking the ignorant person's firm belief, 'this must be done and I will reap its result'; the knower instead works alongside, diligent, and gets them to do their duties.
Do not confuse such aspirants by telling them of another way besides Karma Yoga; by your own work, show that Karma Yoga alone leads to the self and kindle their love of action.
Joṣayet comes from √juṣ, 'to take pleasure, to serve': make them perform. Shake their minds and they lose faith in action without gaining knowledge, falling from both.

The wise carry more responsibility because others copy them. Rather than unsettling beginners with teachings they cannot yet use, they should inspire them to keep doing their duties carefully, since quitting work without real knowledge leaves people with neither.

verses.devanagari:
प्रकृतेः क्रियमाणानि गुणैः कर्माणि सर्वशः ।
अहङ्कारविमूढात्मा कर्ताहमिति मन्यते॥
verses.transliteration:
prakṛteḥ kriyamāṇāni guṇaiḥ karmāṇi sarvaśaḥ
ahaṅkāravimūḍhātmā kartāhamiti manyate
verses.essence: Actions are everywhere performed by the gunas of nature; deluded by ego, one thinks: I am the doer.
verses.translation: All actions are wrought in all cases by the qualities of Nature only. He whose mind is deluded by egoism thinks, "I am the doer."

anvaya.form: present passive participle, neuter, nominative plural (being done)

anvaya.meaning: one whose mind is deluded by ego
anvaya.base: अहङ्कार + विमूढ + आत्मन् · ego + deluded + self
anvaya.parts: अहङ्कार (I-maker, ego) + विमूढ (bewildered) + आत्मा (mind, self): 'one whose self is bewildered by ego'

verses.explanation: The metaphysical floor under detachment. Digestion, heartbeat, even deliberation run on nature's three strands: prakṛteḥ kriyamāṇāni, nature performing everywhere. Then the ego — ahaṅkāra, the 'I-maker' — rushes in to sign the work, and the self deluded by it, ahaṅkāra-vimūḍhātmā, says 'I am the doer.' That claim is not a fact but a stamp applied after the fact: ahaṅkāra is identification with the body and organs whose activity it is. Seeing this loosens the deepest knot of all, ownership of action. The Gita returns to this diagnosis later (13.29, 18.16), because few truths are so easily forgotten.
verses.connection: Supplies the inner mechanics that make 3.25's unattached action possible: the doer was always partly a fiction.
verses.reflection: Once today, mid-action, whisper 'the gunas are moving among the gunas' — and feel the doer relax.
verses.background: If the wise must act just as the ignorant do, what difference remains between them? Śrīdhara presents this verse and the next as the answer. This first verse describes the ignorant one, who becomes attached to action.
verses.hook: Who is really doing your actions when you think you are the doer?

views.text: The guṇas here are their products, the body and organs; ahaṅkāra is identifying with that aggregate, so the deluded person takes its activities, secular and scriptural, as his own.
Ahaṅkāra is applying the notion 'I' to the workings of prakṛti, which is not the 'I'; ignorance of the self's real nature makes one claim the guṇas' deeds.
Actions are done by the strands sattva and the rest; the fool binds himself needlessly by the wrong notion 'I am the doer'.

Every action is carried out by the body-mind mechanism made of material nature; the soul only feels like the doer because ego makes it identify with the body. Yet the soul stays responsible, like a driver directing horses.

verses.devanagari:
तत्त्ववित्तु महाबाहो गुणकर्मविभागयोः ।
गुणा गुणेषु वर्तन्त इति मत्वा न सज्जते॥
verses.transliteration:
tattvavittu mahābāho guṇakarmavibhāgayoḥ
guṇā guṇeṣu vartanta iti matvā na sajjate
verses.essence: But the knower of the truth of guna and action, Mahabaho, understands: gunas move among gunas — and is not attached.
verses.translation: But he who knows the Truth, O mighty-armed (Arjuna), about the divisions of the qualities and (their) functions, knowing that the Gunas as senses move amidst the Gunas as the sense-objects, is not attached.

anvaya.parts: तत्त्व (truth, reality) + वित् (knower): 'one who knows the truth'
महा (great) + बाहु (arm): 'one whose arms are mighty'

anvaya.meaning: about the divisions of guṇas and actions
anvaya.base: गुण + कर्मन् + विभाग · quality + action + division
anvaya.form: compound, masculine, genitive dual (about the two)
anvaya.parts: गुण (quality) + कर्म (action) + विभाग (division): 'the two divisions, of guṇas and of their actions'

verses.explanation: The seer's formula in three words: guṇā guṇeṣu vartante — strands acting upon strands, senses (made of gunas) meeting objects (made of gunas), nature conversing with itself. Once the whole transaction is seen as nature-on-nature, there is no surface left for attachment to stick to. The witness watches the weather happen to the weather.
verses.connection: States positively what 3.27 stated as delusion: the same event, correctly attributed, no longer binds.
verses.reflection: Watch one strong reaction arise and label it nature-meeting-nature; keep the witness seat.
verses.background: Krishna has just described how the deluded person takes himself to be the doer. This verse, the second half of the answer to how the wise and the ignorant differ, turns to the one who knows the truth.
verses.hook: How does someone who knows the truth stay unattached while acting?

views.text: The guṇas in the form of the organs act on the guṇas in the form of their objects; it is they, not the Self, that move, and seeing this the knower does not cling.
The knower frees himself with the view: prakṛti is acting, so what of it reaches me?
The two divisions are 'I am not made of guṇas' and 'the actions are not mine'; one who knows both does not insist on being the doer.
Those who know the truth have dropped bodily identification, so they see every activity as the movement of nature's qualities rather than their own doing, and credit God as the real doer.

verses.devanagari:
प्रकृतेर्गुणसम्मूढाः सज्जन्ते गुणकर्मसु ।
तानकृत्स्नविदो मन्दान्कृत्स्नविन्न विचालयेत्॥
verses.transliteration:
prakṛterguṇasammūḍhāḥ sajjante guṇakarmasu
tānakṛtsnavido mandānkṛtsnavinna vicālayet
verses.essence: Those deluded by nature's gunas are attached to the gunas' workings. The complete knower should not unsettle these dull, partial knowers.
verses.translation: Those deluded by the qualities of Nature are attached to the functions of the qualities. The man of perfect knowledge should not unsettle the foolish one who is of imperfect knowledge.

anvaya.meaning: to the workings of the guṇas
anvaya.parts: गुण (strands) + कर्म (actions): 'the actions of the guṇas'
अ (not) + कृत्स्न (whole) + विद् (knower): 'not knowers of the whole'

anvaya.form: adjective used as noun, masculine, accusative plural (object)

anvaya.parts: कृत्स्न (whole, all) + वित् (knower): 'one who knows the whole'

anvaya.base: वि + √चल् · to move; causative: to shake

verses.explanation: The teaching-ethic of 3.26 returns at the metaphysical level: the doership-illusion, too, must not be torn from people who still need it to function. Telling a struggling worker 'you were never the doer' produces paralysis, not freedom. Truths have prerequisites; the kṛtsna-vit waits for them.
verses.connection: Pairs with 3.26 to bracket the guna-teaching (3.27–28) in compassion: deep truths, gently held.
verses.reflection: Be gentle with those still fully identified with their roles — you were there yesterday.
verses.background: Krishna is still speaking to Arjuna, having just said that the qualities of nature do all the acting and that the knower of truth stays unattached. Śrīdhara introduces this verse as rounding off the earlier warning (3.26) not to unsettle the understanding of those still attached to their work.
verses.hook: Why are people attached to their work, and how should the wise respond?

views.text: The knower of the whole is the knower of the Self; unsettling the beliefs of those intent on results is itself the disturbance he must avoid.
The great man should himself remain in Karma Yoga while contemplating the self as non-agent; the self's agency comes from contact with the guṇas and finally rests with the Supreme Person.
Let the ignorant first do actions for their fruits, and turn them gradually toward selfless work and its purifying benefit.

The ignorant, bewildered by nature's qualities, work for sensual and mental enjoyment. The knowing should not tell them their duties are pointless, but guide them to keep working and slowly rise above attachment.

verses.devanagari:
मयि सर्वाणि कर्माणि संन्यस्याध्यात्मचेतसा ।
निराशीर्निर्ममो भूत्वा युध्यस्व विगतज्वरः॥
verses.transliteration:
mayi sarvāṇi karmāṇi saṃnyasyādhyātmacetasā
nirāśīrnirmamo bhūtvā yudhyasva vigatajvaraḥ
verses.essence: Surrendering all actions to me, with mind on the Self, free of longing and 'mine', fight — with the fever gone.
verses.translation: Renouncing all actions in Me, with the mind centred in the Self, free from hope and egoism, and from (mental) fever, do thou fight.

anvaya.base: सम् + नि + √अस् · to lay down, entrust

anvaya.parts: अध्यात्म (concerning the Self) + चेतस् (mind): 'with a mind turned to the Self'
निर् (without) + मम (mine): 'one with no sense of mine'

anvaya.form: imperative, 2nd person singular, middle voice (a command)

anvaya.parts: विगत (departed) + ज्वर (fever, anguish): 'one whose fever has gone'

verses.explanation: The chapter's instructions converge into one charged sentence, and the word mayi, 'in Me', quietly changes everything: renunciation finally has an address. Mayi sarvāṇi karmāṇi saṃnyasya: the acts are not dropped but deposited, and the self keeps working as trustee, not owner. Adhyātma-cetasā, with mind on the Self; nirāśīr nirmamaḥ, no hoping, no 'mine'; and then yudhyasva, fight. Vigata-jvaraḥ, the fever gone, names Arjuna's actual disease: not the war, but the burning grip around it. Karma-yoga is complete here: the same battle, with ownership transferred and the fever gone.
verses.connection: Gathers 3.9's yajna, 3.19's non-attachment and 3.27's non-doership into a single command — with Krishna as the receiving altar.
verses.reflection: Place this morning's work in higher hands before beginning, and fight your day fever-free.
verses.background: Having said that even the knower must go on acting, Krishna turns to Arjuna himself. Śrīdhara gives the reason: Arjuna is not yet a knower of truth, so action is still his part. The chapter's teaching is now gathered into a direct order to him.
verses.hook: How should you act once you offer all your work to God?

views.text: Adhyātma-cetasā is the discriminating thought 'I am an agent working for God as a servant'; vigata-jvara means free of remorse.
The self is the Lord's body and is moved by him from within, so offer every act as his worship; the fever to drop includes anxiety about one's beginningless store of sin.
Fight for the world's good, renouncing all acts in the Lord with the conviction that he alone is the doer and 'I am nobody'.

This summarises the teaching: keep the mind on God, dedicate every act to him as a sacrifice, give up claims of ownership and craving for results, and take no personal credit, since he supplies the energy for all work.

verses.devanagari:
ये मे मतमिदं नित्यमनुतिष्ठन्ति मानवाः ।
श्रद्धावन्तोऽनसूयन्तो मुच्यन्ते तेऽपि कर्मभिः॥
verses.transliteration:
ye me matamidaṃ nityamanutiṣṭhanti mānavāḥ
śraddhāvanto'nasūyanto mucyante te'pi karmabhiḥ
verses.essence: Those who constantly follow this teaching of mine, full of faith and without cavil, are released even from actions.
verses.translation: Those men who constantly practise this teaching of Mine with faith and without cavilling, they too are freed from actions.

anvaya.form: present participle with negative, masculine, nominative plural (not finding fault)

verses.explanation: The promise, with two conditions worth noticing: śraddhā, trust enough to actually try it, and anasūyā, freedom from the fault-finding spirit that critiques a path as a substitute for walking it. Practice, not perfection, releases.
verses.connection: Closes 3.30's command with its guarantee — and the temperament it requires.
verses.reflection: Practice this teaching one day with full faith, uncavilling, and judge it by the evening.
verses.background: Krishna has just told Arjuna to fight with every act surrendered to him. Śrīdhara presents this verse as the reward of acting in that way, now stated for anyone who takes up the teaching, not only for Arjuna.
verses.hook: What happens to those who follow this teaching with faith?

views.text: Anasūya means not detracting from Vasudeva the teacher; such followers are freed from actions called righteous and unrighteous alike.
Api ('even they') marks three groups, all released: those who practise, those who have faith but do not yet practise, and those who at least do not cavil.
Not cavilling means not faulting the teaching for pushing one into painful action; such people, working slowly, are freed like the fully knowing.
Accepting the teaching with faith and living by it calms the mind's fever of lust, anger and greed and frees one from karmic bondage. Krishna humbly calls his universal principle merely his opinion.

verses.devanagari:
ये त्वेतदभ्यसूयन्तो नानुतिष्ठन्ति मे मतम् ।
सर्वज्ञानविमूढांस्तान्विद्धि नष्टानचेतसः॥
verses.transliteration:
ye tvetadabhyasūyanto nānutiṣṭhanti me matam
sarvajñānavimūḍhāṃstānviddhi naṣṭānacetasaḥ
verses.essence: But those who, carping, do not follow this teaching — know them, blind to all knowledge, mindless, lost.
verses.translation: But those who carp at My teaching and do not practise it, deluded of all knowledge, and devoid of discrimination, know them to be doomed to destruction.

anvaya.form: present participle, masculine, nominative plural (while finding fault)

anvaya.base: सर्व + ज्ञान + विमूढ · all + knowledge + bewildered
anvaya.parts: सर्व (all) + ज्ञान (knowledge) + विमूढ (deluded): 'deluded in every kind of knowledge'

verses.explanation: The counterpart, stated without softening. Asūyā — the carping that finds reasons not to begin — does not merely delay growth; it corrodes the faculty that grows. One can disagree with a teaching and remain whole; one cannot sneer at every teaching and remain whole.
verses.connection: The shadow of 3.31: the same teaching, met with cavil instead of faith, and the two destinations.
verses.reflection: Notice where you carp at wisdom you have not yet tried — critique without practice is a closed door.
verses.background: Having spoken of those who follow his teaching with faith, Krishna turns to the opposite case. Śrīdhara calls it the fault on the other side: those who resent the instruction that work is to be done for the Lord and refuse to carry it out.
verses.hook: What happens to those who reject this teaching and find fault with it?

refs.note: Defines faith as firm conviction in God and Guru even before one understands their words, the attitude the commentary says this verse demands.

views.text: Those who decry this instruction and do not follow it are deluded in various ways about all knowledge, lack discrimination, and should be known as already gone to ruin.
'My teaching' is that the self has the Lord as support, is subservient to him and moved by him; those who reject it lack the mind's very function, judging things as they are.
Those with no faith in this knowledge are lost because they stay soaked in the fear of birth and death.
The teaching being decried is that action should be done for the Lord's sake; its scorners are deluded about both action and Brahman.

Our limited intellect cannot grasp everything, so faith is needed: where we cannot understand, we accept and keep practising. Pride makes people reject what they cannot comprehend, and so they ruin themselves by refusing the path to liberation.

verses.devanagari:
सदृशं चेष्टते स्वस्याः प्रकृतेर्ज्ञानवानपि ।
प्रकृतिं यान्ति भूतानि निग्रहः किं करिष्यति॥
verses.transliteration:
sadṛśaṃ ceṣṭate svasyāḥ prakṛterjñānavānapi
prakṛtiṃ yānti bhūtāni nigrahaḥ kiṃ kariṣyati
verses.essence: Even the knower acts according to his own nature; beings follow nature — what will repression accomplish?
verses.translation: Even a wise man acts in accordance with his own nature; beings will follow Nature; what can restraint do?

anvaya.form: adjective used as adverb, neuter, accusative singular (in accordance)
pronoun-adjective, feminine, genitive singular (of his own)
noun, feminine, genitive singular (with 'in keeping with')
adjective used as noun, masculine, nominative singular (subject)

verses.explanation: A startling concession at the chapter's edge: even knowledge does not erase temperament — the wise act through their nature, not despite it. Nigraha, brute suppression, is declared nearly powerless against the current of svabhāva. The path forward is not damming the river but learning, in the next verse, where its rapids are.
verses.connection: Tempers the chapter's confidence: technique meets the stubborn fact of one's given nature.
verses.reflection: Stop warring with your basic temperament today; redirect the river, do not lecture it.
verses.background: Krishna has just condemned those who reject his teaching. A question follows, which Śrīdhara spells out: if the reward is so great, why does not everyone restrain the senses, give up desire and keep to their own duty? This verse begins the answer.
verses.hook: Why can't even a learned person simply suppress their own nature?
