views.text: Nature means the impressions of past virtue, vice and the like that become manifest at the start of this life; the obvious worry, that scripture and effort become pointless, is answered in the next verse.
Even one who knows the self as distinct from prakṛti acts toward objects by old impressions; what can scripture's discipline do against them on its own?
Do not conclude that human effort has no scope; the next verse shows one can master nature by rising above attraction and aversion.

Everyone is driven by tendencies from past lives, so forced repression backfires. The practical path is to accept where we stand and redirect the force of our nature toward God, doing our duty as service.

verses.devanagari:
इन्द्रियस्येन्द्रियस्यार्थे रागद्वेषौ व्यवस्थितौ ।
तयोर्न वशमागच्छेत्तौ ह्यस्य परिपन्थिनौ॥
verses.transliteration:
indriyasyendriyasyārthe rāgadveṣau vyavasthitau
tayorna vaśamāgacchettau hyasya paripanthinau
verses.essence: Attraction and aversion sit stationed in each sense toward its object. Come not under their sway — they are the two ambushers on the road.
verses.translation: Attachment and aversion for the objects of the senses abide in the senses; let none come under their sway; for, they are his foes.

anvaya.form: noun, neuter, genitive singular (repetition means 'each and every')

anvaya.parts: राग (attraction) + द्वेष (aversion): 'attraction and aversion', the pair

anvaya.base: वि + अव + √स्था · to be settled, placed

anvaya.form: pronoun, masculine, genitive dual (of the two)

verses.explanation: If nature cannot be repressed (3.33), where is freedom? Here: not in the senses' contact with objects — that is nature's business — but in the pull-and-push installed at each contact point. Rāga and dveṣa are paripanthinau, highway robbers stationed along every perception. One cannot close the road; one can refuse to hand them the reins.
verses.connection: Answers 3.33's pessimism with the precise location of choice: between the sensation and the surrender to it.
verses.reflection: Mark your two tripwires — the like and the dislike planted in each sense — and step over one.
verses.background: Krishna has said that beings follow their nature and that restraint achieves little. That raises a worry Śaṅkara states plainly: if everyone acts only from nature, there is no room for personal effort and scriptural instruction becomes pointless. Krishna answers by showing where effort still has room.
verses.hook: Where do your likes and dislikes come from, and must you obey them?

views.text: Here is the scope for effort: control love and hatred by their opposite, discrimination, and one follows scripture instead of being led by nature; they are robbers blocking the way to liberation.
Even after some control of the senses, these two drag the aspirant on the path of knowledge back into action toward objects, so they are his unconquerable foes.
Nature pulls the careless along like a deep current once attraction and aversion arise; scripture acts earlier, engaging one in worship of the Lord, which blocks them.

We still need sense objects to maintain the body; the task is not to stop using them but to stop being ruled by the attraction and aversion they create. Freed from likes and dislikes, we act from our higher nature.

verses.devanagari:
श्रेयान्स्वधर्मो विगुणः परधर्मात्स्वनुष्ठितात् ।
स्वधर्मे निधनं श्रेयः परधर्मो भयावहः॥
verses.transliteration:
śreyānsvadharmo viguṇaḥ paradharmātsvanuṣṭhitāt
svadharme nidhanaṃ śreyaḥ paradharmo bhayāvahaḥ
verses.essence: Better one's own dharma, though flawed, than another's well performed. Death in one's own dharma is better; another's dharma invites fear.
verses.translation: Better is one's own duty, though devoid of merit than the duty of another well discharged. Better is death in one's own duty; the duty of another is fraught with fear (is productive of danger).

anvaya.parts: स्व (one's own) + धर्म (duty, law): 'one's own dharma'

verses.explanation: The chapter's most quoted and most arguable verse. Arjuna's flight would not land him in 'no role' but in someone else's: the renunciate's, for which he has neither the nature nor the ripeness, and lived falsely even a holy part corrodes the actor. Svadharme nidhanaṃ śreyaḥ, even death in one's own dharma is better: the verse's hardest clause, and the tradition keeps it hard. Readings range from social station to the path one is fit for, but all converge on the warning: para-dharma is bhayāvahaḥ, fear-bringing, because a borrowed life must be continuously defended. Better to die as yourself than flourish as a copy.
verses.connection: Caps 3.33–34: since nature cannot be escaped, align with your own — Arjuna's exit was never an exit, only a costume change.
verses.reflection: Choose your own rough-edged path once today over a borrowed polished one, and notice the rightness.
verses.background: Arjuna has said (2.5) he would rather live on alms than fight. Śrīdhara frames this verse for such a person: one who finds his own duty, here war, painful and hard to do perfectly, and is drawn to another's duty, such as non-violence, that seems easier and just as righteous.
verses.hook: Is it better to do your own duty imperfectly or another's well?

views.text: One's own duty, even defective, is better than another's well performed; even death in it is better than living in another's duty, which is fraught with fear because it invites dangers such as hell.

One's own dharma is Karma Yoga, natural and easy and not liable to lapse; Jnana Yoga, though done well for a while, is another's. Dying unfinished on one's own path does not matter: the next birth carries it on.
One's own duty is rooted in the heart as a natural taste; no creature is born without it, so it should not be given up.
Arjuna is tempted by non-violence, another's dharma, as easier and equally virtuous; but death in his own dharma of battle leads upward, while the forbidden path leads to hell.

One's own dharma, suited to one's nature and stage of life, can be done with a steady mind. Taking up another's duty because it looks attractive creates inner disharmony and hinders spiritual progress.

verses.speaker: अर्जुन उवाच
verses.devanagari:
अथ केन प्रयुक्तोऽयं पापं चरति पूरुषः ।
अनिच्छन्नपि वार्ष्णेय बलादिव नियोजितः॥
verses.transliteration:
atha kena prayukto'yaṃ pāpaṃ carati pūruṣaḥ
anicchannapi vārṣṇeya balādiva niyojitaḥ
verses.essence: Arjuna asks: then by what is a person impelled to sin, Varshneya, even unwilling — as if engaged by force?
verses.translation: But impelled by what does man commit sin, though against his wishes, O Varshneya (Krishna), constrained as it were, by force?

anvaya.form: present participle with negative, masculine, nominative singular (not wanting)

anvaya.base: नि + √युज् · to attach; causative: to compel
anvaya.form: causative past participle, masculine, nominative singular

verses.explanation: The question every honest person eventually asks: why do I do what I do not want to do? Anicchann api — even against the will — names the universal experience of being overridden from inside. Arjuna has stopped asking about the war; he is asking about the saboteur.
verses.connection: Provoked by 3.34's ambushers: if they are stationed in every sense, what exactly are they?
verses.reflection: Ask Arjuna's question of your last regret: what pushed me, as if by force?
verses.background: Arjuna breaks in for the first time since his questions at the chapter's start. Krishna has told him not to fall under the sway of attraction and aversion; as Śrīdhara reads him, Arjuna doubts this is possible, since people do wrong even while resisting, and suspects a deeper force behind it.
verses.hook: What drives people to do wrong even when they don't want to?

views.text: Impelled as a servant is by a king: the question asks what that commanding cause is.
The question concerns the aspirant on the path of knowledge who, against his own resolve, is dragged into experiencing sense objects.
Even people who check desire and anger by discrimination fall back into sin, so Arjuna suspects some deeper root behind those two.
Arjuna voices a universal struggle: our conscience, rooted in the soul's kinship with God, tells us what is sinful, yet some force pushes us into it anyway. He wants that force named.

verses.speaker: श्रीभगवानुवाच
verses.devanagari:
काम एष क्रोध एष रजोगुणसमुद्भवः ।
महाशनो महापाप्मा विद्ध्येनमिह वैरिणम्॥
verses.transliteration:
kāma eṣa krodha eṣa rajoguṇasamudbhavaḥ
mahāśano mahāpāpmā viddhyenamiha vairiṇam
verses.essence: It is desire, it is anger, born of the guna of rajas — all-devouring, greatly sinful. Know this to be the enemy here.
verses.translation: It is desire, it is anger both of the quality of Rajas, all-devouring, all-sinful; know this as the foe here (in this world).

anvaya.base: रजस् + गुण + समुद्भव · passion + quality + origin
anvaya.parts: रजः (passion) + गुण (strand) + समुद्भव (arising): 'arising from the strand of rajas'
महा (great) + अशन (food, eating): 'one whose eating is enormous'

verses.explanation: The indictment names one criminal with two faces: kāma eṣa krodha eṣa, desire is this, anger is this. Anger is only desire obstructed (the chain of 2.62 compressed); treat the symptom and the root re-sprouts. Born of rajas, it is mahāśanaḥ, the great eater: no satisfaction retires it, and feeding it is how it grows. It is mahāpāpmā too, the great sinner, the push behind wrongdoing. Krishna gives Arjuna at last an enemy he can fight without grief: it is not across the field.
verses.connection: Answers 3.36 by name — and quietly relocates the war from Kurukshetra to the interior.
verses.reflection: Name the enemy precisely next time: not the person, not the situation — the wanting, and its anger.
verses.background: Krishna, called here the Blessed Lord, replies to Arjuna's question of 3.36: what pushes a person into wrong against his will? Śrīdhara notes that anger, named apart from desire earlier in the chapter, is now treated together with it, since desire that is blocked turns into anger.
verses.hook: What is the enemy that pushes people into wrongdoing?

views.text: Rajoguṇa-samudbhava can also mean 'the source of rajas': once desire arises it stirs rajas and drives a person into action, which is why the sufferer says 'desire made me do it'.
'This' said twice shows desire and wrath are not different; mahāśana is taken as 'devourer of the feast', that is, of happiness.
It cannot be bought off, being insatiable (mahāśana), nor reconciled, being fierce (mahāpāpmā); so it must be killed, and it wanes as sattva grows and rajas declines.

Desire for worldly enjoyment, a distorted form of the soul's love for God, is the root of sin. Satisfied desire breeds greed, frustrated desire becomes anger, and all three lead people into wrongdoing.

verses.devanagari:
धूमेनाव्रियते वह्निर्यथादर्शो मलेन च ।
यथोल्बेनावृतो गर्भस्तथा तेनेदमावृतम्॥
verses.transliteration:
dhūmenāvriyate vahniryathādarśo malena ca
yatholbenāvṛto garbhastathā tenedamāvṛtam
verses.essence: As fire is covered by smoke, a mirror by dust, an embryo by the womb — so is this covered by that.
verses.translation: As fire is enveloped by smoke, as a mirror by dust, and as an embryo by the amnion, so is this enveloped by that.
verses.explanation: Three veils of three thicknesses: smoke, which a breeze clears; dust, which needs wiping; the womb, which only time and birth remove. Desire obscures the inner light in all three grades — sometimes a passing haze, sometimes ground-in habit, sometimes a covering only a whole rebirth of the person dissolves. Diagnosis includes severity.
verses.connection: Grades the enemy of 3.37: not all coverings of knowledge are equal, nor cleared by the same effort.
verses.reflection: Find which veil covers your clarity today — light smoke, thick dust, or full womb-darkness.
verses.background: Having named desire as the enemy, Krishna now shows, as Śaṅkara puts it, how it is an enemy, through three pictures of something covered. The verse leaves open what 'this' is that desire covers; the next verse says.
verses.hook: How does desire hide what you already know is right?

views.text: Fire, naturally bright, is covered by smoke born together with it; likewise a mirror by dirt and a foetus by the amnion. So 'this' is shrouded by desire; what 'this' means is taken up next.
What is covered is the embodied beings themselves, enveloped by desire.
The three similes show three sides of the foe: a harmful appendage, a maker of mischief, and an object of disgust; 'this' that is covered is the Self.
The three images are three kinds of covering: smoke is born with the fire, dirt comes from outside, and the membrane encloses the embryo on every side.

Desire clouds the intellect's power to tell right from wrong, in three grades: light like smoke over fire, heavier like dust on a mirror, total like a womb covering an embryo. Sensual pleasure makes us forget our perilous position.

verses.devanagari:
आवृतं ज्ञानमेतेन ज्ञानिनो नित्यवैरिणा ।
कामरूपेण कौन्तेय दुष्पूरेणानलेन च॥
verses.transliteration:
āvṛtaṃ jñānametena jñānino nityavairiṇā
kāmarūpeṇa kaunteya duṣpūreṇānalena ca
verses.essence: Knowledge is covered by this eternal enemy of the knower — by desire, the insatiable fire, Kaunteya.
verses.translation: O Arjuna, wisdom is enveloped by this constant enemy of the wise in the form of desire, which is unappeasable as fire.

anvaya.parts: काम (desire) + रूप (form): 'having desire as its form'

verses.explanation: Two epithets complete the profile. Nitya-vairī, the constant enemy of the knower: the fool greets desire as a friend until sorrow arrives, but the wise see the harm even while the wanting lasts, so for them it is never anything but an enemy. And duṣpūra anala, the fire that cannot be filled, for whom every offering is fuel. An enemy that feeds on satisfaction cannot be satisfied into peace.
verses.connection: Deepens 3.37–38: why appeasement fails — the covering is made of appetite itself.
verses.reflection: Feed a craving and watch it grow; skip feeding it once and watch it complain, then quiet.
verses.background: The previous verse ended on a riddle: 'this is covered by that'. Śaṅkara frames this verse as the answer to what 'this' is, the thing desire hides. Krishna is still answering Arjuna's question about what drives people to sin, and here calls him Kaunteya, son of Kuntī.
verses.hook: Why can't desire ever be satisfied by feeding it?

refs.note: The Buddha says even a rain of coins cannot satisfy desire; the wise know desire brings little joy and much pain, echoing the verse's insatiable fire.

views.text: Anala, fire, is explained as 'that which never has enough (alam)'; desire is the constant enemy of the wise alone, who feel its pull as harm from the start.
Duṣpūra, hard to fill, is read as fixing on things not worth gaining; and it never reaches satisfaction.
Kāmarūpa means 'looking like something desired', since it works through wanting; like fire it burns up both the visible and the unseen fruits of good deeds.
Desire is an insatiable fire that overpowers even the wise; every attempt to satisfy it makes it burn stronger, so a life spent chasing its fulfilment is wasted.

verses.devanagari:
इन्द्रियाणि मनो बुद्धिरस्याधिष्ठानमुच्यते ।
एतैर्विमोहयत्येष ज्ञानमावृत्य देहिनम्॥
verses.transliteration:
indriyāṇi mano buddhirasyādhiṣṭhānamucyate
etairvimohayatyeṣa jñānamāvṛtya dehinam
verses.essence: The senses, the mind and the understanding are its seat; through these it deludes the embodied, veiling knowledge.
verses.translation: The senses, the mind and the intellect are said to be its seat; through these it deludes the embodied by veiling his wisdom.

anvaya.form: pronoun, neuter, instrumental plural (by means of)

anvaya.base: वि + √मुह् · to be confused; causative: to bewilder

verses.explanation: Intelligence on the enemy's positions: desire garrisons three strongholds in ascending depth — the sense-gates, the mind that savors, the very buddhi that is supposed to judge. The last is the alarming one: when the judge is occupied, desire issues its commands in the voice of reason.
verses.connection: Maps the territory before the battle-plan of 3.41: know where the enemy is quartered.
verses.reflection: Locate where desire garrisons in you — senses, mind, or intellect — and visit the outpost.
verses.background: Krishna has described desire as the enemy that covers knowledge. Śaṅkara explains why he now tells where it lives: once an enemy's base is known, it can be destroyed easily. This verse and the next go together, first the seat, then the remedy.
verses.hook: Where does desire live within you?

views.text: The activities of the organs are the channels through which desire expresses itself; by stirring them it covers the knowledge of the Self.
Senses, mind and intellect, made servants by attachment, become desire's instruments for turning the self from its own nature toward sense pleasures.
Anger rises first at the sense organ when the enemy is seen, then in the mind as fancy, then in the intellect as resolve; so delusion builds and knowledge is destroyed.

Naming desire's strongholds, the senses, mind and intellect, is the first step to defeating it. These instruments are not bad in themselves; they were given for reaching God and must now be used to lift ourselves.

verses.devanagari:
तस्मात्त्वमिन्द्रियाण्यादौ नियम्य भरतर्षभ ।
पाप्मानं प्रजहि ह्येनं ज्ञानविज्ञाननाशनम्॥
verses.transliteration:
tasmāttvamindriyāṇyādau niyamya bharatarṣabha
pāpmānaṃ prajahi hyenaṃ jñānavijñānanāśanam
verses.essence: Therefore, Bharatarshabha, first govern the senses and slay this evil destroyer of knowledge and discernment.
verses.translation: Therefore, O best of the Bharatas (Arjuna), controlling the senses first, do thou kill this sinful thing, the destroyer of knowledge and realisation.

anvaya.parts: भरत (Bharata's line) + ऋषभ (bull, chief): 'bull among the Bharatas'

anvaya.base: प्र + √हन् · to strike down (some read √हा, to abandon)
ज्ञान + विज्ञान + नाशन · knowledge + realization + destroying
anvaya.parts: ज्ञान (knowledge) + विज्ञान (realized wisdom) + नाशन (destroyer): 'that which destroys both knowledge and realization'

verses.explanation: Strategy follows the map: ādau, *first*, at the outermost gate — the senses — where the enemy is weakest and the fight cheapest. One does not begin the war in the citadel of buddhi; one begins at the walls. Krishna ends a teaching on desirelessness with a command to kill: even renunciation, rightly understood, is a warrior's act.
verses.connection: Converts 3.40's intelligence into orders: engage at the perimeter, before desire reaches the command center.
verses.reflection: Regulate the senses first thing today; win the border before the capital is contested.
verses.background: Krishna has just named the senses, the mind and the intellect as desire's dwelling place. Now he draws the practical conclusion for Arjuna, addressing him as best of the Bharatas. Śrīdhara reads this as the second of a pair: after the seat comes the means of victory.
verses.hook: Where should you begin if you want to overcome desire?

views.text: Prajahi means 'renounce, cast off'; jñāna is learning from scripture and teacher, vijñāna its full experience, the two means to liberation that desire destroys.
'First' means at the very start of the practice for release: regulate the senses through Karma Yoga, then destroy desire.
Jñāna-vijñāna-nāśana can be read as how to kill it: by thought and by higher thought, that is, do not let anger born in the senses enter fancy, and form no resolve about it.

We create desires ourselves and then suffer the agitation they cause, mistaking relief for happiness. Seeing ourselves as the soul makes it easier to curb the senses and slay the desire living in them.

verses.devanagari:
इन्द्रियाणि पराण्याहुरिन्द्रियेभ्यः परं मनः ।
मनसस्तु परा बुद्धिर्यो बुद्धेः परतस्तु सः॥
verses.transliteration:
indriyāṇi parāṇyāhurindriyebhyaḥ paraṃ manaḥ
manasastu parā buddhiryo buddheḥ paratastu saḥ
verses.essence: The senses are high, they say; higher than the senses, the mind; higher than the mind, the understanding; and beyond the understanding — That.
verses.translation: They say that the senses are superior (to the body); superior to the senses is the mind; superior to the mind is the intellect; one who is superior even to the intellect is He (the Self).

anvaya.form: noun, neuter, accusative plural (object of 'they say')
verb, perfect (with present sense), 3rd person plural

verses.explanation: The chain of command, ascending: objects, above them the senses, above the senses the mind, above the mind the buddhi, and above all, the Self. Desire fights downhill, capturing the lower links; the seeker must fight uphill, each level disciplining the one below from the strength of the one above. The summit of the chain is the one thing desire cannot garrison — the Self that watches even the buddhi.
verses.connection: Supplies the architecture for 3.41's campaign: where reinforcements come from at each level.
verses.reflection: Climb your own chain of command once: sensation, mind, intellect — and greet what stands above them all.
verses.background: Krishna has told Arjuna to restrain the senses and cast off desire. Śaṅkara poses the question this verse answers: relying on what can one give desire up? Krishna replies by ranking the inner faculties one above another.
verses.hook: What is higher than the senses, the mind and the intellect?

views.text: Each is higher in subtlety, inwardness and pervasiveness; 'he' beyond the intellect is the supreme Self, the witness of the intellect, the embodied one whom desire deludes.
'Saḥ' is desire itself: even if senses, mind and intellect fall quiet, desire born of rajas can stir them again, so it stands as the strongest obstacle to self-knowledge.
The senses illuminate the body and objects, the mind drives the senses, the intellect's decision precedes the mind's will, and beyond it is the Self as their inner witness.
A lower faculty can be governed by a higher one: senses above the body, mind above the senses, intellect above the mind, and the soul above all. This ladder is the tool for uprooting desire.

verses.devanagari:
एवं बुद्धेः परं बुद्ध्वा संस्तभ्यात्मानमात्मना ।
जहि शत्रुं महाबाहो कामरूपं दुरासदम्॥
verses.transliteration:
evaṃ buddheḥ paraṃ buddhvā saṃstabhyātmānamātmanā
jahi śatruṃ mahābāho kāmarūpaṃ durāsadam
verses.essence: Thus knowing That beyond the understanding, steadying the self by the Self, slay, Mahabaho, this enemy in the form of desire, so hard to assail.
verses.translation: Thus knowing Him Who is superior to the intellect and restraining the self by the Self, slay thou, O mighty-armed Arjuna, the enemy in the form of desire, hard to conquer.

anvaya.parts: काम (desire) + रूप (form): 'having desire as its form'
दुर् (hard) + आसद (reaching, getting hold of): 'hard to get hold of'

verses.explanation: The chapter closes its ring: it opened with Arjuna asking why he must do this terrible work, and ends with Krishna commanding jahi śatrum, slay the enemy, now correctly identified. Evaṃ buddheḥ paraṃ buddhvā: know what stands beyond even the intellect. Saṃstabhyātmānam ātmanā: steady the self by the Self, the only leverage that works against an enemy quartered inside, since desire cannot be beaten at its own level. The war Arjuna must not flee was never primarily the one in front of him.
verses.connection: Seals 3.36–42 and the whole chapter: act, unattached, and turn the warrior's strength on the real adversary.
verses.reflection: Slay one small desire today by the Self's authority, not by willpower's white knuckles.
verses.background: Chapter 3 ends here. Arjuna asked (3.36) what drives people to sin against their will; Krishna has named desire, shown where it hides and ranked the faculties up to the Self. He now addresses Arjuna as mighty-armed for the final instruction, which Śrīdhara marks as the conclusion.
verses.hook: How do you finally defeat desire that seems unconquerable?

refs.note: The chariot image: soul as passenger, body the chariot, intellect the driver, mind the reins, senses the horses. The awakened soul must steer, as this verse urges.

views.text: Ātmanā is read as the purified mind: with it, establish the Self firmly in absorption; desire is hard to grasp because its ways are inscrutable.
What lies beyond the intellect is desire, the foe of Jnana Yoga; fix the mind by the intellect in Karma Yoga and destroy it.
Beyond the intellect is the supreme I-consciousness, 'I am all', which nothing can frustrate, so anger cannot rise there; take hold of that energy of consciousness and slay the foe.
Desire and its kin are changes in the intellect, while the Self is their changeless witness; steady the mind with that firm conviction and kill the enemy.
Since the soul is divine, no material object can satisfy it. Knowing this, the soul should train the intellect to rein in the mind and senses, as the passenger of a chariot directs its driver.
